fable-5.1.text:
I think value functions are going to be important, and I think there is a reason why they haven't been quite as important as they should be, which has to do with the way RL is being done right now.

So let me say what a value function is, because maybe not everyone knows. When you're doing RL, the way it works right now with these models is you give the model a task, and the model goes and does a very, very long rollout. It thinks for a long time, maybe it uses tools, and at the end you get a reward. Did it succeed or did it fail. And then you learn from that. The learning only happens at the end of the whole episode.

A value function is something that lets you say, in the middle of the rollout, how well is this going. Are we on a good track or a bad track. And if you have a good value function, you don't need to wait until the end to learn. You can learn from a mistake the moment you make it.

The way I like to think about it is, suppose you are proving a theorem, and you spend a thousand steps doing something, and then you realize this approach is hopeless. A person realizes that quite early. They don't need to go all the way to the end and fail and then say, okay, I will update on this. They say, I spent a few steps on this, this is clearly not working, and that realization is itself the training signal. And I think evolution did something like this with us. Emotions are something like a value function. You feel bad about something before the consequences arrive. That is a very useful thing to have. It's compressed, it's hardwired, and it lets you learn from much shorter horizons.

The reason it hasn't been so important is that if the episodes are short enough and you can do enough of them, you can get away without it. You just do the rollout and get the reward. But as the tasks get longer, and I think they will get much longer, the end-of-episode signal becomes very sparse relative to the number of decisions you make. So I would expect the value function to be, let's say, a bigger part of the story. Not the only thing, but I think it's one of those things where when you look back you'll say, of course, how could it have been otherwise.

opus-5.5.text:
I think value functions are going to be quite important, and the way to see why is to look at how reinforcement learning is done today.

Right now, the typical setup is that the model does a very long thing. It thinks for a long time, takes a lot of actions, maybe tries to solve some hard problem, and only at the very end does it get a score: did it work or not? Then that signal is used to update everything that came before. It's quite inefficient. If the trajectory is long, you learn nothing until you reach the end.

What a value function lets you do is short-circuit that wait. It tells you, partway through, whether you're doing well or badly. Chess is a simple example. If you lose a piece, you know you made a mistake, and you don't need to play the whole game to find out. In something like math or programming, suppose you've been going down some direction for a while, and you realize it's not going to pan out. A good value function would give you that signal right then, at the moment you decide the direction is unpromising. That lets you learn from the decision that led you there, not just from the final outcome.

People sometimes say value functions are hard to learn, and that's true. But I think there's something deep there. Look at people. Humans have something like a value function that is very robust, and I'd argue a lot of it comes from emotions. Emotions tell you, in a very fast and rough way, whether things are going well or badly. There are these cases where someone has damage to the part of the brain that processes emotion. They stay articulate and can still reason about puzzles. But they become extremely bad at making decisions. They'll take hours deciding which socks to put on, and they'll make terrible choices in their lives. So this simple, hardcoded value signal turns out to be essential for functioning well in the world.

So my expectation is that value functions will be used more and more. Strictly speaking, anything you can do with a value function you can also do without one. It's just going to be slower, sometimes much slower. And as we try to make these systems learn more efficiently, more like people do, I think having good value functions will be a big part of how that happens.

fable-5.text:
I think value functions are going to be important, but maybe let me explain what a value function is for the people who are listening. When you do reinforcement learning, the way reinforcement learning works right now in LLM training is that you have your model try to solve a problem through some long trajectory — maybe thousands or tens of thousands of actions, lots of thinking — and only at the very end do you get a score. Did it work or did it not work. And then the learning signal comes from that final outcome and gets propagated back through the whole trajectory.

The value function is the idea that you shouldn't have to wait until the end. You could have some way of saying, midway through, "how is it going?" An intuitive example: suppose you're trying to prove some theorem, and after some amount of effort you realize the approach is unworkable — the whole direction is flawed. You should be able to get a learning signal right at that moment of realization. You don't need to finish the trajectory to know you made a mistake, and the mistake was made much earlier, when you committed to the bad approach. So the value function lets you short-circuit the wait and make learning much more efficient, because the signal attaches closer to the decision that actually mattered.

This is well established in some domains. The TD-learning that was used for backgammon long ago, and the way systems like AlphaZero work — those rely on value functions very heavily. In chess it's very natural: if you lost a piece without compensation, you don't need to play the game to the end to know things went badly.

I'll also point out there's a case to be made that in people, emotions are something like value functions. They're this evaluation of how things are going that's fast, that's somewhat hardwired, and that shapes your behavior long before you see final outcomes. If something bad happens, you feel it immediately, and that feeling does a lot of the work of teaching you. The interesting thing is that these are relatively simple — the emotional reactions, the value functions of people — yet they seem quite robust and they serve us pretty well across very different situations from the ones we evolved in.

So will value functions play a role? I expect so. I think whatever people are doing right now, which from the outside appears to be mostly end-of-trajectory rewards, is leaving something on the table in terms of efficiency. But I'd also say the value function is more of an efficiency gain than a fundamental change — anything you can learn with a value function, you can in principle learn without one, just more slowly. The more fundamental questions about how these models generalize, I think, lie elsewhere.

opus-5.text:
I think value functions are underutilized right now, and that they will become more important. Let me explain what I mean.

The way RL is done today with these models is essentially Monte Carlo. You take your model, you have it do some long trajectory — hundreds of actions, thousands of tokens — and then at the very end you find out whether it worked or not, and you propagate that single scalar back across everything the model did. That's a valid way to learn. It's just very inefficient in terms of how much signal you extract per unit of compute.

A value function is the claim that you don't have to wait until the end. If you're playing chess and you lose your queen for nothing, you don't need to play out the remaining forty moves to know that something went wrong. You know right away. If you're doing a math proof and you've gone down a path where you've made some unjustified assumption, you can tell at that moment that your probability of success just dropped a lot. And then you want to learn from that moment, rather than from the eventual failure a thousand tokens later.

I also think there's something interesting here about emotions. Emotions look to me a lot like a value function — a fairly low-dimensional, hard-coded-by-evolution value function that gives you continuous feedback about how things are going. And it's notable that it's low-dimensional, because that probably makes it more robust, harder to fool.

The caveat is that value functions are harder to get right than they sound. If your value function is confidently wrong, it will cut off the exploration that would have taught you something. Some of the best ideas look terrible for a while. So you want something that gives you intermediate signal without being so sure of itself that it prunes away the thing you needed to discover. I don't think that's solved. But I'd be surprised if the eventual systems didn't have something playing that role.

sonnet-5.5.text:
I think value functions will matter a lot. Right now, the way RL is done, you give a model a problem and it goes off and thinks, or takes actions, for a very long time. Only when it produces a solution do you evaluate it, and that final score becomes the training signal for every step along the way. So you can spend thousands of steps going down some path and learn nothing until the very end. That's quite wasteful.

What a value function does is short-circuit that. It tells you, partway through, whether you're doing well or badly, without waiting for the end. Take chess. If you lose a piece, you know right away that something went wrong. You don't need to play out the whole game to learn that. Or take programming or math. Say you explore one direction for a thousand steps and conclude it's a dead end. With a good value function, the signal that this was a bad direction can come back at the moment you started down it, not only when you finally fail. That would make learning much more efficient.

People often say value functions are hard to learn, or that you can do without them, and in some settings you can. But I don't see a fundamental reason they should be unusable. I'd put it as something that isn't central in today's approaches but that I expect to become more important.

There's also something about people here that I find interesting. Emotions seem to play the role of a kind of built-in value function. There's a well-known case of someone who lost their emotional processing through brain damage. They stayed articulate and could solve puzzles, but became terrible at making even simple decisions, like which socks to wear. That suggests this kind of internal "how am I doing" signal is doing a lot of work in making us effective, and it's quite robust across a wide range of situations. I think something analogous will be important for machine learning.

haiku-5.5.text:
I think they're going to matter a lot more than they do right now. Most of reinforcement learning today works by letting the model run all the way to the end of a task, seeing whether it got the right answer, and then adjusting. That's wasteful. If you're on a long reasoning chain and you've clearly gone wrong somewhere in the middle, you should be able to notice that before you've spent the whole thing.

A good value function gives you that signal along the way. It tells you whether the direction you're heading is promising, so you can learn from partial progress instead of only from the final result. When you have a strong sense of how things are going at each step, the learning gets much more efficient.

There's a human analogy I find useful. Emotions work a bit like value functions. If you make a decision and feel bad about it right away, that feeling guides you long before the consequences fully play out. Evolution seems to have built that in deliberately. For models, I think we're still early in figuring out how to build that kind of intermediate judgment well, and I suspect that's where a lot of the next gains will come from.

astra-6.text:
I think value functions are going to be important. The reason is that, if you’re doing something that takes many steps, you would like to know whether you’re making progress before you reach the end.

Think about chess. You could evaluate a move by playing the entire game and seeing who wins. But if you have a good value function, you can look at the position and say, “This looks promising.” That lets you spend your computation much more effectively.

Now imagine you’re working on a difficult problem. You try an approach, you spend some time on it, and then you have to decide: should I keep going, or should I try something else? A value function is a way of making that decision. It’s an intuition about whether the current situation is likely to lead to success.

The difficulty is learning an intuition that’s actually reliable. If you’re doing something unfamiliar, your estimate might be wrong. You might abandon an approach just before it would have worked. So a value function doesn’t eliminate the need to explore or to check your work.

But broadly, as we ask systems to do longer tasks and spend more computation solving problems, I would expect the ability to judge intermediate progress to become increasingly useful.

sol-6.1.text:
I think value functions will be very important. The basic reason is that, if you are doing something which takes a long time, you would like to get some indication of whether you are making progress before you reach the end.

Suppose you are trying to solve a difficult problem. You explore an approach for a while, and then you think, “Actually, this is not going anywhere.” You stop and try something else. You haven’t solved the problem, but you’ve made a useful judgment. A value function is a way of learning that kind of judgment: given where I am now, how promising is this situation?

That can help both with learning and with deciding where to spend computation. You don’t want to pursue every possible direction equally. You want to develop an intuition for which directions are worth pursuing.

Of course, the difficulty is that the judgment itself can be wrong. An approach can look very promising and lead nowhere. Or the essential step can look unpromising until you understand it. So the value function needs to improve together with the system’s ability to solve problems. But I would expect learned judgments about intermediate progress to become increasingly useful as the tasks become longer.

sol-6.text: I think value functions will be very important. It’s one thing to generate possible actions; it’s another to recognize which ones are likely to lead somewhere good. A good value function could guide planning and learning without requiring the system to follow every path to the end. The difficult part is making that judgment reliable over long horizons and in situations the system hasn’t seen before.

terra-5.6.text: I think value functions are going to be extremely important. They let you learn from outcomes rather than just imitate the next token or action, and that gives a system a way to reason over longer horizons. My guess is that as models become more capable, the central problem will be learning really good value functions—ones that capture what we actually want and can generalize far beyond the situations they were trained on.

sol-5.6.text: I expect value functions to play a very large role. A value function is, in some sense, an intuition about whether a situation is promising—whether the current line of reasoning is likely to lead to a good outcome. If you have a sufficiently good value function, you don’t need to search blindly through an enormous number of possibilities; you can direct computation toward the paths that are most likely to work. That seems essential for reasoning over long horizons, where the reward arrives only at the end and individual intermediate steps are difficult to evaluate.

luna-5.6.text:
I think value functions will become increasingly important. At a high level, intelligence is not just predicting what happens next; it’s predicting the consequences of possible actions and understanding which outcomes are desirable. That is essentially what a value function represents.

Today, value functions are mostly used in reinforcement learning to guide policy improvement. But as models become more capable, I expect them to play a much broader role: evaluating long-horizon plans, guiding search, deciding which computations are worth performing, and perhaps helping systems learn from sparse or delayed feedback. The difficult part is that the value function has to capture what we actually care about, rather than some convenient proxy. So learning useful and robust value functions may be one of the central problems in building advanced AI.

luna-6.text: I think value functions are going to be very important, because they let a system reason about how promising a situation is before it has reached the end. If you only learn from the final outcome, you get a very sparse signal. A value function gives you a way to evaluate intermediate steps, compare possible paths, and focus computation where it’s likely to help. It may not always exist as a neat, separate component; it could be part of the model’s internal representations. But some ability to estimate future potential seems essential for building systems that can plan and learn efficiently.
